en: The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatācintyaviṣayāvatāra Sūtra, one fascicle,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty,
by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying beneath the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of Magadha, having attained perfect enlightenment.

That Bodhi tree was named Aśvattha; its roots were deep and firm, its trunk rose straight upward, and it was perfectly round and without knots, like a pillar of sandalwood—upon which birds would wheel their wings, none being able to pass over it; its bark was fine and smooth, with various colors shining forth, like patterned silk.
Its leaves are dense and verdant, its branches spreading far and wide;
all around it, wondrous flowers are in full bloom, radiating brilliance and wafting fragrance,
so exceedingly delightful that they are peerless, with the exception of the *kubjaka-paricchattra* tree.
Furthermore, it was surrounded by immeasurable small trees.
This king of trees, lush, verdant, and preeminent, was like Mount Sumeru, towering above all other peaks; for a distance of one yojana, there was nowhere it could not be seen by all.
Fragrance wafted everywhere and radiant light shone forth; from afar at night, one gazing upon it would mistake it for a great mass of fire.

Beneath it was solemn and magnificent, like the Garden of Joy (Nandana); on all four sides it was level and open, with fragrant grasses growing luxuriantly, as beautiful and sweet-smelling as the ruffled neck-feathers of a peacock king, such that those who beheld it could never tire.
The Tathāgata sat here with dignified majesty, surrounded by the great assembly like the moon among the stars.

At that time, Buddhas from other directions, as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, manifested in the form of bodhisattvas and came to sit in the assembly, desiring to adorn the maṇḍala of Vairocana.

Their names were: Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, Bodhisattva Su-tejorāśi, Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Mahāmati, and Bodhisattva Samantabhadra; these and others such as them were the leaders among the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable thousands of billions of bodhisattvas who manifested in the forms of śrāvakas and also came to sit in the assembly.

Their names were Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Rāhula, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Upāli, Aniruddha, Revata, Ānanda, Devadatta, Upananda, and others as their leaders. All of them had long practiced the six pāramitās and were close to the Buddha’s bodhi; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they manifested in the forms of śrāvakas within this defiled land.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable thousands of bhikṣuṇīs, with Mahāprajāpatī as their leader; all had already accomplished the deeds of a Great Man, yet they manifested in female bodies for the sake of taming inferior sentient beings.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable Śakras, Brahmās, Lokapālas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; all among them were great bodhisattvas, with none who were ordinary beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat beneath the Bodhi tree, solemn, pure, and sublime, like a wish-fulfilling jewel placed beneath a *citraka* tree; with right mindfulness, he remained unmoving, like Mount Sumeru.

In order to cause the assembly of bodhisattvas and all sentient beings to understand the profound, secret meditative concentration and the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, he entered a samādhi named "The Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata."

At that moment, within each of the thirty-two marks of the World-Honored One, there appeared immeasurable Buddha-fields of the ten directions and those Buddhas therein, just as various forms are reflected in a clear mirror.

Furthermore, within each of the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), there again appeared all the difficult and ascetic practices the Tathāgata had performed while cultivating the bodhisattva path—from the time he was King Prabhāsa until his final encounter with Dīpaṃkara Buddha—including the complete relinquishing of his head, eyes, body, skin, flesh, hands, feet, wife, children, servants, as well as his royal throne, palace, and other possessions.
Because this samādhi possesses great power, all Buddhas constantly enter this meditative concentration at the times of eating, walking, preaching the Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa.

Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas rely upon this samādhi to accomplish immeasurable great majestic powers, even to the point of realizing the emptiness of all phenomena, and are thus able to manifest various kinds of sovereign deeds throughout all Buddha-fields in the ten directions.
For example, it is like a person who dreams of various transformations and such things; once they have awakened, what was seen is entirely non-existent.
Ordinary beings are likewise: because of the dream of ignorance, they falsely conceive of all phenomena as having substantial reality.

Having attained awakening, all Buddhas are entirely free from attachment; therefore, throughout all worlds in the ten directions, they can manifest immeasurable Buddha-activities in a single thought-moment with sovereign non-obstruction, benefiting and bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment, so that they may all awaken to and enter immeasurable, profound, and wondrous gates of liberation.
At that time, because the Bodhisattva Guṇakośa had not yet fully perfected his practice of the bodhi-path, he asked the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra:
"What is the name of the samādhi into which the Tathāgata has now entered?"
"Furthermore, how can one manifest various Buddha-activities throughout all worlds in the ten directions to deliver and liberate sentient beings?
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Guṇagañja Bodhisattva, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"I shall now explain it for you.
At that time, the bodhisattvas gazed up at him with single-minded devotion and said in unison:
"Excellent is this question!"
"It is profound and subtle; the Venerable Samantabhadra, who possesses all-knowing vision, shall now expound it.
At that moment, the great earth shook in six ways, the heavens rained down exquisite flowers, and the afflictions and manifold sufferings of all sentient beings were briefly stilled.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
This samādhi is named 'The Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgatas'; it is the bodhi of all Buddhas, for all Tathāgatas constantly rely upon and abide within it."

Ever since the World-Honored One first received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he has entered this samādhi; constantly and effortlessly, he spontaneously manifests immeasurable buddha-activities. That is to say, within a single hair-tip of space, there are as many buddha-worlds as there are atoms in all buddha-fields.

Within this, he may manifest birth in the Tuṣita heaven, or passing away from there, descend and enter a womb; or manifest being born and taking seven steps, declaring, "I am now at the very limit of birth and death"; or manifest dwelling in the palace, leaving home, and practicing austerities; or manifest subduing Māra, attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, and turning the sublime wheel of Dharma; or manifest remaining in the world for immeasurable kalpas to deliver all sentient beings, causing them all to leave suffering behind; or again manifest entering into nirvāṇa; or make all kalpas into a single kṣaṇa, or a single kṣaṇa into all kalpas—such that kalpas and kṣaṇas neither increase nor decrease.

Until all sentient beings have attained complete liberation, he constantly performs such various Buddha-activities throughout all these worlds at every single moment, never resting, and doing so without effort.

Just as within a single hair-tip’s worth of space in the void, throughout immeasurable lands, the various majestic demeanors and dharmic rules of all Buddhas are universally manifested in every thought-moment without effort;
even so it is throughout the entirety of space, down to the measure of a single hair-tip.

Furthermore, within every single atom of all those lands, there are again lands exceeding in number the atoms of all Buddha-lands; and within each of these lands, in every single kṣaṇa, the majestic deportment and activities of all Buddhas are spontaneously and universally manifested—whether appearing in celestial palaces or even entering final nirvāṇa—thereby liberating immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings.

In this manner, from moment to moment until the end of the future, they constantly perform the work of Buddhas to benefit sentient beings; even until the realm of sentient beings within the void is exhausted, they never cease, yet the Buddha-fields do not diminish and the atoms do not increase.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are like illusions and mirages, lacking any solidity.

For example, the great assembly of bodhisattvas in this gathering—equal in number to the atoms within ten buddha-worlds—all dwell together here in this land of Magadha, spanning twelve yojanas, without obstructing one another.

Each and every atom therein likewise receives countless Buddha-worlds—whether upright, inverted, facing one another or turned away, or situated side by side, or even interpenetrating one another without obstruction—and it is just so.
It is like a person in a dream who sees various things in a single location; because they are not real, there is no obstruction.

All these lands are nothing other than manifestations of one's own mind. Whether one sees the conflagration at the end of an eon, or that it has already been consumed by fire, or that it is formed by wind, or whether it is pure or defiled, or even devoid of a Buddha—all such diverse differences are seen by sentient beings according to their own mental karma.
For example, when hungry ghosts, driven by hunger and thirst, go to the Ganges, some see water, while others see ashes, pus and blood, or excrement and urine, filled with impurities.
Sentient beings are likewise; each, according to their own karma, perceives that Buddha-land as either pure or defiled,
as the Buddha being present in the world or having entered nirvana, as dwelling at the site of enlightenment preaching the Dharma for the assembly,
as hearing the teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), or again hearing the praise of the Dharma of giving, or seeing [the Buddha] practicing.
They may see him standing, or sitting and eating; or they may see his body one, two, up to seven times the height of a worldly person;
or one *yojana*, a hundred *yojanas*, or a thousand *yojanas* tall; or they may see his majestic radiance like the newly risen sun, or like the full moon;
or, due to karmic obstructions, they may encounter the Buddha, the World-Honored One, after a long time has passed.
Regarding parinirvāṇa, there are some who do not even hear the names of the Buddhas;
they are like those hungry ghosts who, amidst the Ganges River, see no water at all, but only various kinds of impure filth.
Some see various Buddhas, each coming from their own native lands, manifesting in the forms of majestic great bodhisattvas and entering this assembly.
In one land, sentient beings see only the conflagration of the kalpa-fire; in another land, sentient beings are filled to capacity, and all together behold the Buddha.

Or one may see the Tathāgata gathering all lands into a single Buddha-land, and placing a single Buddha-land into all lands; it is like those with cataracts who, in the same location, perceive various distinct differences that do not obstruct one another, all due to their visual impairment preventing them from seeing true colors.
Sentient beings are likewise: the nature of form is unimpeded, yet because the objects of the mind differ, they are obscured from right view and fail to understand reality.
"O Son of the Buddha!

I shall now briefly explain for you the method of abiding in this samādhi. Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, abides in this samādhi, within a single thought-moment he pervades the entire realm of space—even in places the size of a hair-tip—reaching immeasurable Buddha-lands, and within every single atom of those lands, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in a dharma-realm. For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, moment by moment, he pervades each and every world, manifesting the skillful means, dignified conduct, and activities of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-lands."
In this manner, until all sentient beings have fully realized unsurpassed bodhi, it shall never cease.

Just as it is with this one Buddha, so too it is with the second, the third, and indeed with all Buddhas throughout the ten directions; the great power of majestic virtue manifested by each and every one of them is likewise thus.

At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Guṇakara attained this samādhi while still upon his seat. He immediately beheld those immeasurable Buddhas and came to know the majestic power and skillful means of those Buddhas; by the power of this samādhi, he was likewise able to discipline and transform sentient beings.
A multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of a hundred Ganges Rivers, each individually realized various samādhis, patiences (*kṣānti*), and stages (*bhūmi*).

Because the great bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara, who abide in the ten stages, have fully perfected their meritorious virtues and sublime practices, they have all long ago attained this samādhi. Within a single kṣaṇa, they encompass immeasurable kalpas; within a single atom, they contain immeasurable lands; and within a single thought-moment, they pervade all realms, constantly and effortlessly manifesting the deeds of the Buddhas through spontaneous presence.
Although they hear this Dharma, they make no further progress.
It is like a full bottle placed in the rain; it cannot contain even a single drop. These bodhisattvas are just like this.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was in samādhi, he emitted from between his eyebrows a light named "Great Manifestation. All bodhisattvas who still practiced with effort and had not yet realized the ten stages, having encountered this light, all beheld within the air, upon every tip of a hair, and within every minute atom, immeasurable buddha-fields—just as a white mustard seed contained within a crystal jar is seen by any observer. The bodhisattvas likewise saw all the buddha-fields within the minute atoms in this same manner.

Furthermore, they behold all the Buddhas of those lands; within the body of each and every Buddha, they see the bodies of all Buddhas. Each of these Buddhas possesses immeasurable names, and for the sake of benefiting each and every sentient being, they constantly and spontaneously manifest throughout every single Buddha-land in every thought-moment, attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is like placing a wish-fulfilling jewel upon a high banner, which naturally rains down all kinds of precious treasures, satisfying the intentions of sentient beings according to their needs.
The Tathāgata is likewise; manifesting perfect enlightenment, he naturally delivers and liberates immeasurable sentient beings.

The sentient beings within these various lands are each distinct from one another, yet they do not obstruct each other, just as one who possesses supernormal powers travels through space without being hindered by mountains, rivers, rocks, or walls.
Why is this? Because all realms of existence are like illusions and mirages, lacking any solid reality.

Having perceived this, the assembly of Bodhisattvas each saw their own bodies pervading all lands; before each Buddha, within a single thought-moment, they paid respectful homage and made offerings for one kalpa, two kalpas, three kalpas, or even hundreds of thousands of kalpas, or for as brief a duration as a single thought-moment or a single instant.

Or they may hear the Buddha preach the various *pāramitās* and *dhāraṇī* gates, or speak of the various stages (*bhūmis*), or manifest spiritual transformations by entering all eons into a single thought-moment; thereby conceiving a sense of profound wonder and rarity, they think to themselves:

"How is it that the World-Honored One, with his majestic virtue and sovereign power, in a single instant enables me to fulfill the roots of goodness and merit accumulated over immeasurable eons, so that I may swiftly realize the Tathāgata’s inconceivable realm-samādhi and its great majestic spiritual power?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakośa, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, again asked the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra:
"For those who wish to realize this samādhi, what merit, generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom should they cultivate?"

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, who had manifested the attainment of perfect enlightenment throughout all pure lands in the ten directions to transform sentient beings, addressed the Bodhisattva Guṇakara, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

If one wishes to realize this samādhi, one should first cultivate merit and accumulate all roots of goodness. This means constantly making offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, as well as to one's parents; and regarding all those who are impoverished, afflicted by suffering, without protection or refuge, and worthy of compassion, one should embrace them and not abandon them, even to the point of not begrudging one’s own flesh and body.
Why is this? Those who make offerings to the Buddha attain great merit and virtue, swiftly accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and cause all sentient beings to obtain peace and happiness;
those who make offerings to the Dharma increase their wisdom, realize mastery over the Dharma, and are able to correctly understand the true nature of all phenomena.
Those who make offerings to the Sangha increase their immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom, thereby attaining the path of Buddhahood.

One should likewise provide offerings to one's parents, preceptors, and venerable teachers, as well as to those in the world who have previously provided benefit and whose kindness one relies upon; mindful of this, one should redouble one's offerings as an act of gratitude.
Why is this? Because those who recognize their debt of gratitude, even while remaining within the cycle of birth and death, do not destroy their roots of goodness;
whereas those who do not recognize their debt of gratitude sever their roots of goodness and commit all manner of evil deeds.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas praise those who recognize kindness and censure those who betray it.
Furthermore, they constantly take pity upon and rescue sentient beings suffering in various ways; by means of these vast roots of goodness, the bodhisattva never regresses or loses them.
If a person is able to diligently cultivate merit, constantly mindfully repay kindness, and feel compassion for sentient beings, then Bodhi is already in their hands.
One should know that the Buddha taught that by making offerings according to these three types of fields, one will individually accomplish immeasurable roots of goodness.
“Guṇākara, you should know that a bodhisattva must next plant vast seeds; from these, the sprouts of this samādhi arise, which bring about the fruit of awakening.
How does one plant these seeds?

That is to say, one holds various exquisite flower garlands, ointments, powdered incenses, and manifold musical instruments to reverently make offerings to the Buddhas currently present, or to their images, while reflecting:

"As previously described, throughout the entirety of space—even within the tip of a hair and inside a single atom—there are immeasurable lands; in each of these, I see the majestic power of all Buddhas and their assemblies of Bodhisattvas. Within all those Buddha-assemblies, I shall, with a single mind and right mindfulness, universally make offerings to them all."
Just as the dharma-nature of one Buddha is the dharma-nature of all Buddhas, so if I make an offering to one Tathāgata, it is an offering to all Tathāgatas.

"According to the spiritual power of each and every one of those Buddhas, one can enter as many eons into a single thought-moment; likewise, for that many eons, one shall make offerings to the Tathāgatas.
If there are sentient beings who believe and understand this Dharma and plant the great seeds, they will immediately be able to attain this vast Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable realm.
Therefore, son of good family!

You should make offerings with this Dharma every day; by doing so, even if you merely pay a single prostration upon reaching the presence of the Buddhas, you will be able to cause these seeds to grow and the sprouts of samādhi to emerge.
Furthermore, one should constantly irrigate it with generosity, ethical discipline, great vows, and wisdom.

Moreover, when a bodhisattva practices generosity for the sake of irrigating samādhi, they do not discriminate between fields of merit, enemies or kin, good or evil, those who maintain precepts or break them, or the wealthy and the poor.
Furthermore, he reflects:
"Although giving to the wealthy may be of no use to them, I myself ought to practice the perfection of generosity.

Moreover, the Bodhisattva should maintain pure ethical discipline; upon seeing those who violate their precepts, he should give rise to great compassion and should not harbor feelings of aversion or anger toward them.
Furthermore, one should deeply resolve upon the Great Bodhicitta Vow:

"I shall, with certainty, in every thought-moment, throughout all places as vast as the tip of a hair that fill space, and even within all the infinite worlds amidst the dust motes of every Buddha-field, attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, turn the wondrous Wheel of Dharma, and deliver all sentient beings—just like the present World-Honored One, Vairocana, without any difference—and without exerting effort, I shall condense immeasurable eons into a single thought-moment."

"Then, within each of these individual lands, he manifests as many Buddha-activities as there are atoms in a Buddha-field; in each activity, he delivers as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, causing them all to leave suffering behind, continuing without rest until the realm of sentient beings throughout space is exhausted."
“O Son of the Buddha!
You who cultivate wisdom, listen attentively with a single mind; I shall now speak for you.
If a good man or a good woman, seeking unsurpassed bodhi, resolves their mind to realize this samādhi, that person must first cultivate wisdom, because this samādhi is attained through wisdom.”

One who cultivates wisdom should distance themselves from false speech, frivolous talk, and all distracting or unbeneficial matters; though they give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, they should constantly restrain the mind so that it remains unstained and undistracted.

He went into the vihāra and beheld the image of the Buddha, adorned with a golden hue, some fashioned entirely of gold, its physical marks complete; immeasurable transformation Buddhas entered into samādhi, seated in succession within a circular halo.
Then, prostrating with his head at the feet before the image, he reflected thus:

"I have heard that there are currently in the world immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, namely: the Buddha Sarvārthasiddha, Amitābha Buddha, Ratnaketu Buddha, Akṣobhya Buddha, Vairocana Buddha, Ratnacandra Buddha, Ratnaprabhāsa Buddha, and others."
Toward those Buddhas, in accordance with one’s own inclinations and in places of veneration, one should give rise to great pure faith.

One should visualize the forms of the Buddhas as the actual bodies of those Tathāgatas, honoring and respecting them as if seeing them before one’s eyes, observing them from head to foot with single-minded concentration and without distraction.

Go to a secluded place and sit upright in contemplation, as if the Buddha were present before you at a distance of one hand-span; keep your mind constantly focused on him so that you do not forget, and if you should momentarily forget, you should go back to observe him again.

When observing in this manner, one gives rise to a heart of supreme reverence and respect, as if the Buddha’s true body were manifest before one; seeing it with perfect clarity, one no longer conceives of it as a mere image.

Having seen them, one should immediately, at the place of those Buddhas, respectfully circumambulate them to the right with exquisite flower garlands, powdered incense, and unguents, making various kinds of offerings.
He should thus fix his mind with single-minded attention, as if the World-Honored One were always dwelling before him.
For the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who sees all, hears all, and knows all, fully knows my mind.
Having thus repeatedly visualized the manifestation until it is perfected, one returns to a secluded place and binds the mind before oneself so as not to let it be lost.
Practicing with single-minded diligence for three weeks, a person of merit will immediately see the Tathāgata appearing before them;

however, those who have created obstacles through evil karma in previous lives and are unable to see him may still quickly behold him if they can practice with single-minded diligence without regressing or entertaining other thoughts.
Why is this? If one seeks unsurpassed bodhi and practices with single-minded devotion toward even a single matter, there is nothing that will not be accomplished.
If, however, one repeatedly falters and retreats from what is being practiced, such a person cannot even attain liberation for themselves, let alone deliver all suffering sentient beings.

If one encounters such [teachings] yet fails to diligently cultivate them in order to swiftly attain the path of true and correct enlightenment, you should know that this person is merely a heavy burden upon the earth.
It is like a person who, having drunk a single handful of water from the great ocean, claims to have already drunk all the waters of every river in Jambudvīpa.

In this way, if a bodhisattva can cultivate this ocean of enlightenment, they have already cultivated all samādhis, all patiences, all stages, and all dhāraṇīs. Therefore, one should always practice diligently without laziness, remain free from negligence, and bind the mind in single-minded concentration, so as to personally attain the vision of the Buddha before one's eyes.
Cultivating in this manner, when first seeing the Buddha, one reflects:
"Is this the true Buddha,
or is it a physical image?"

If you know that what you see is the true Buddha, then before the Buddha, with both knees touching the ground and palms joined in reverence, you should call to mind all the Buddhas throughout the measure of space as fine as a hair-tip and within every atom, and because of their immeasurable majesty and great compassion, they have appeared before you;
you should then make this request: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound for me the Dharma of the Great Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Inconceivable Realm."
"If you hear anything spoken by the Tathāgata, you should believe it with certainty and not give rise to doubt; thus, in that very moment, you will attain this samādhi.
If, due to karmic obstructions from previous lives, you are unable to ask questions, you should reflect:
'All dharmas are like illusions, like mirages, like cataracts, like shadows, like reflections, and like dreams. In this way, contemplate the emptiness and quiescence of the nature of phenomena."

However, I know that the Tathāgata understands all phenomena to be like illusions and dreams; yet the self-nature of the Tathāgata is neither illusion nor dream, being like empty space. Since you are able to manifest before me through wisdom and compassion, I pray that you will emit the great compassionate blue light for me and extinguish all sufferings.

At that time, the Buddha immediately emitted a light from between his eyebrows called "Blue Flame. As soon as the light shone upon them, all their sufferings were eliminated; they sat and realized the patience of the light of Dharma (*dharmaprabhāsa-kṣānti*), and were able to fully comprehend immeasurable samādhis.
On the seventh night, he dreamed that the Tathāgata bestowed upon him the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If one knows that what was seen was merely an image, one should reflect that all Buddhas and all sentient beings are likewise like images; they are perceived only according to one's thoughts and lack any substantial nature.

Having realized that the Tathāgata is like an illusion, like a transformation, like a dream, and like a mirage, one thus naturally perceives the Buddha appearing before them; yet this is like a dream, wherein nothing substantial can be found. He is not born, yet he appears to be born; he does not perish, yet he appears to perish; he does not go, yet he appears to go; he is not consciousness, yet he is perceived as consciousness; he is not conditioned, yet he manifests all formations (*saṃskāra*); he is not speech, yet he expounds all dharmas; he is not a self, not a life-principle, not a sentient being, not a nourisher, not one who transmigrates, not perception, not an agent, not a knower, and not a consumer. He is not identical with the aggregates (*skandha*), nor does he abide within the aggregates, yet he demonstrates the aggregates; even so it is with the elements (*dhātu*) and the sense-bases (*āyatana*).
All things are neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, the Buddhas and all dharmas are truly equal, sharing the same single characteristic, like a mirage and so forth.
All sentient beings, all Buddhas, and all their lands are manifested solely through the conceptualizations of one's own mind-consciousness.
With consciousness and conceptualization as conditions, the various forms that arise are ultimately non-existent.
The Tathāgata has already transcended all perceptions of consciousness; therefore, one should not perceive him through physical forms or images.

One should know that perceived images arise in accordance with conceptualization. This applies even to every true Buddha, from those as vast as space to those as minute as a hair-tip; they are all likewise like empty space—equal and without distinction.

If one discriminates, one perceives the Buddha; if one is free from discrimination, there is nothing perceived. The Buddha is created by one's own mind; apart from the mind, there is no Buddha. Even all the Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise thus: they are all non-existent, existing only in dependence upon one's own mind.

If a bodhisattva can thoroughly understand that all Buddhas and all phenomena are merely the measure of mind, they will attain the patience of conformity (anulomikī-kṣānti) or enter the first stage (prathamā bhūmi). Thereupon, they will cast off their body and be swiftly reborn in the world of Abhirati, or be born within the pure Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī, where they constantly behold the Tathāgata and personally receive his teachings and make offerings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakośa again addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate, and who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe it, how much merit will they obtain?"
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva said:
"Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively!

Suppose there were someone who could gather all sentient beings within the three realms and cause them to be liberated from birth and death, attaining the state of Arhat; and suppose each of those Arhats were individually provided with celestial, exquisite clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions for various offerings throughout a hundred kalpas."
After his parinirvāṇa, one should further erect stūpas made of the seven precious jewels for each [of these teachings] and offer them reverent worship.

Suppose there were another person who, throughout a hundred kalpas, purely maintained the prohibitive precepts, or practiced patience, diligence, and meditative concentration; although this person would obtain immeasurable merit, it would not equal that of someone who hears this Dharma-gate, receives it with respect and faith, and does not give rise to slander. The latter’s merit surpasses the former, and they will swiftly attain perfect enlightenment.
At that time, all the immeasurable Buddhas from all the lands of the ten directions manifested their own bodies and praised Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“O Son of the Buddha!
It is as you have said.

At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni emitted rays of light of immeasurable colors from his face, which illuminated the three realms of existence everywhere; various kinds of flowers rained down, wondrous music played spontaneously without being struck, and the great earth trembled slightly.
Within that light, he spoke these verses:
"If one hears this Dharma with a pure mind, One will attain the stages, concentrations, and dhāraṇīs,
As well as mastery in precepts, patience, and supernormal powers, And swiftly realize the unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment."
He turns the wondrous wheel of Dharma never before turned, just as the Great Sages of the past did;
within a single thought-moment he encompasses many eons, and upon a single atom he universally manifests immeasurable lands.
Immeasurable sentient beings are submerged within the three realms, Constantly oppressed and tormented by various sufferings;
Bound by false views and having lost the right path, May they all, in every thought-moment, attain liberation.

Because the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra had long since realized this Dharma-gate, when he spoke it for the sake of the assembly, hundreds of millions of devas and humans were delivered from all suffering, and all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The Bodhisattva Guṇakaraṇḍa and the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as the world’s devas, nāgas, asuras, and others, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
